# Why templates?

Modules 1–3 styled documents *inside* the `.qmd`. That doesn't scale: if ten
colleagues each paste the same show rules, you have ten copies to maintain.
The professional approach is a **template** — style lives in `.typ` files,
content lives in `.qmd` files, and everyone shares the template.

This very document is rendered through the custom template in the
`templates/` folder. Look at the title block above: coloured title, rule
line, styled headings — none of that is defined in this file.

# How Quarto's Typst templates work

Quarto assembles the final `.typ` file from **partials**. The two you
usually override are:

`templates/typst-template.typ`

:   Defines a Typst *function* (ours is called `article`) that takes
    metadata (title, authors, date…) plus the document body, and lays
    everything out. This is pure Typst — no Quarto syntax.

`templates/typst-show.typ`

:   The glue. It contains a Typst `#show` rule that pipes the whole document
    through `article(...)`, filling the arguments from your YAML metadata
    using Pandoc's `$variable$` syntax.

Open both files now in RStudio and read them alongside this explanation —
they are short and heavily commented.

# Passing custom metadata

Anything in your YAML can flow into the template. This document defines a
custom key `brand-color` in its YAML, and `typst-show.typ` forwards it to
the template with:

```
brand-color: rgb("$brand-color$"),
```

Change `brand-color` at the top of this file to `"#8b1f2d"` and re-render:
the title and headings change colour. One knob, whole-document effect.

# Some content to admire

Headings, emphasis and tables all pick up the template's styling
automatically:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demo
#| tbl-cap: "Iris species means."
knitr::kable(
  aggregate(cbind(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length) ~ Species, iris, mean),
  digits = 2
)
```

*Emphasis* is tinted with the brand colour, thanks to a show rule inside the
template — the `.qmd` stayed plain Markdown.

# Distributing a template to colleagues

Three good options, in increasing order of polish:

1. **A repo like this one** — colleagues copy `templates/` next to their
   `.qmd` and add the `template-partials` lines to their YAML.
2. **A Quarto project** — put the `format` block in `_quarto.yml` once;
   every `.qmd` in the project inherits it with a bare `format: typst`.
3. **A Quarto extension ("custom format")** — package the template so users
   can write `quarto use template yourorg/yourtemplate`. See
   <https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst-custom.html>.

# Exercises

## 🏋️ Exercise 4.1 — Rebrand

Change `brand-color` in this file's YAML and re-render. Then move the
setting into the template as the *default*, so documents that don't specify
a colour still look right. (Hint: the `article` function already declares a
default value — find it.)

## 🏋️ Exercise 4.2 — Add a footer

Edit `typst-template.typ` so every page has a footer with the document title
on the left and the page number on the right. Hints: the `set page(...)`
call accepts `footer:`; use `#context counter(page).display()` for the
number, and `#h(1fr)` to push things apart.

## 🏋️ Exercise 4.3 — A subtitle style

The template already receives `subtitle`. Restyle it: make it italic, grey
(`luma(120)`), and 14pt.

## 🏋️ Exercise 4.4 — Project-wide format

Create a `_quarto.yml` in this folder containing the `format: typst` block
with the `template-partials`, then delete the `format:` section from this
file's YAML and confirm it still renders identically.
